The enhancement of the free OH(2) and OH(6) was understandable, because there was the\nbreakage of H-bonds among cellulosic molecules, which resulted in more extensive delamination and\nhigher specific surface area (as shown in Figure S4 and Table S1 in Online Resource). This made cellulose\nmore accessible to water and chemicals. However, for the free OH(2) and OH(6) of hardwood fiber,\nthe number of the free OH(2) and OH(6) decreased by 21.65% from 14.32% to 11.22%, with revolutions\nincreasing from 0 r to 4000 r, followed by an increase of 45.37% in the stage of refining from 4000 r to\n12,000 r, along with an decrease of 17.11%. It could be explained by the instability of free OH groups,\nwhich makes it easy to form new H-bonds, such as O(2)H···O(6) or O(6)H···O(3′)H-bonds. Thus although\nthere is the formation of free OH(2) and OH(6) during fibrillation, the content of the free OH(2) and OH(6)\nmight disease; meanwhile, the content of the O(6)H···O(3′) or the O(2)H···O(6) H-bonds might increase\nupon drying.\n\n3.4. Correlation between CI and Content of Inter-Molecular H-Bonds during PFI Reﬁning\nSimilar to the CI-XI, the content of O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds decreased ﬁrst and then had an increase,\nfollowed by a decline for the two ﬁbers (as shown in Figure 8a,b). Besides, the Pearson correlation\ncoeﬃcients were calculated between the content of H-bonds and the CI-XI. It was 0.912 (p < 0.05)\nfor softwood ﬁbers and 0.889 (p < 0.05) for hardwood ﬁbers, respectively. The similar trends in the\ncontent of the O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds and the CI-XI might be because that the crystalline region has a\nhigher content of O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds when compared with the amorphous regions, as illustrated\nin Figure 9 [35].",
      "Polymers 2020, 12, 2912 11 of 14\n\nFigure 8. The trend of the CI-XI, the CI-XA, and the O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds: (a) softwood ﬁbers and\n(b) hardwood ﬁbers.\n\nFigure 9. The illustration of a two-phase structure of cellulose.\nThe correlation between the CI-XI and the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds or the free OH(2) and OH(6)\nwas poor for the following reasons. The free OH groups are easier for forming the O(2)H· · · O(6)\nH-bonds as opposed to the O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds in the amorphous region, because the distance\nbetween adjacent glucose units in a cellulosic molecular chain is closer than between the glucose units\nin the adjacent molecular chain (as shown in Figure 9). Accordingly, when compared with the content\nof O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds, there was less diﬀerence in the content of the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds or the\nfree OH groups between the crystalline region and amorphous region, which sometimes made the\ncontent of the two bonds not change much in regards to the crystallinity. The O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds\nis stable, as mentioned above. It was presumed to change little as crystallinity changed during PFI\nreﬁning. Hence, the correlation between O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds and the CI-XI was not discussed in the\npresent study.",
      "2.3. Water Retention Value (WRV)\nThe WRV was determined with 0.5 g samples (o.d.) according to ISO 23714.\n(m1 −m2) WRV(%) = × 100% (1)\nm2\nwhere m1 is the weight of the sample after centrifugation and m2 is the weight of the oven-dried sample.\n\n2.4. XRD Analysis\nThe crystallinity of pretreated ﬁbers was determined by a Shimadzu XRD 7000S (Shimadzu,\nKyoto, Japan), while using Cu-Ka radiation. The samples were scanned at 40 kV and 30 mA in a 2θ\nrange of 4–40◦at 1◦/min. It is well known that two polymorphs, cellulose Iα and Iβ, are present in\nnative cellulose; for clarity, all of the reﬂections indexed here are on the Iβ lattice. Before analysis,\nthe experimental data is nine point smoothed with Savitzky–Golay algorithm. The two types of CI\nvalues were obtained from peak intensity method (CI −XI) and peak ﬁtting (CI-XA), respectively.\nThe CI −XI was calculated as in Equation (2) [19].\n(I200 −Iam) CI −XI = × 100% (2)\nI200\nwhere I200 is the maximum diﬀraction intensity value of the (200) lattice plane between the scattering\nangles of 2θ = 22◦and 23◦, and Iam is the minimum diﬀraction intensity of amorphous fraction between\n2θ = 18◦and 19◦.\nAll of the XRD diﬀractograms were smoothed with the Savitzky–Golay algorithm and\nbaseline-corrected with linear ﬁt function. Subsequently, the baseline-corrected diﬀractograms\nwere deconvoluted with the Pearson VII function. The value of the CI-XA equals the area percentage\noccupied by crystalline peaks over the total area of the diﬀraction pattern [20]. In addition, the crystallite\nsize was calculated by the widely used Scherrer Equation (3) [21]:\nk × λ\nL = (3)\n(β × cos θ)\nwhere L is the size that is perpendicular to the lattice plane, k is a constant that depends on the crystal\nshape (0.89), λ is the wavelength of the incident beam in the diﬀraction experiment (0.154 nm), β is the\nfull width at half maximum of the diﬀraction peak, and θ is the Bragg’s angle. In general, the values of\nthe calculated crystallite sizes might be lower than that of the real crystallite sizes, because the peak\nbroadening from the instrumental factors was not considered [22].\n\n2.5. FT-IR Analysis\nTHE FT-IR spectra were recorded on solid samples in KBr pellets by means of an FT-IR Bruker\nVertex 70 spectrometer (Karlsruhe, Germany). Unreﬁned and reﬁned ﬁbers were smashed into powder\nbetween 40 and 60 mesh. Subsequently, the powder sample of each species (5 mg) was dispersed in a\nmatrix of highly pure KBr (500 mg). The spectral was recorded by averaging 64 recordings and at a\nresolution of 4 cm−1 with transmission mode from 4000 cm−1 to 400 cm−1. The results were made on\nthe average spectrum that was obtained from ﬁve recordings.\nThe energy of the H-bonding EH for several OH stretching bands was calculated while using\nEquation (4) [13].\nνo −ν\nEH = (4)\nνo\nνo is the wavenumber corresponding to free OH groups (3650 cm−1), ν is the frequency (cm−1) of\nthe bonded OH groups, and k is a constant (1/k = 2.625 × 102 kJ).",
      "Polymers 2020, 12, 2912 12 of 14\nThe results indicated that the ﬁbrillation and properties of ﬁbers are related to the variation of the\nsupramolecular structure during PFI reﬁning. It is noticeable that there was a signiﬁcantly positive\ncorrelation between the CI-XI and content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds during PFI reﬁning for softwood\nﬁbers and hardwood ﬁbers. Thus, the trend of the content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds might be generally\nspeculated based on CI-XI while reﬁning. Besides, the crystallite size, crystallinity, and content of\nvarious H-bonds did not change much in general. It is assumed that PFI reﬁning is an excellent\nmechanical treatment of ﬁbrillation with relatively little destruction on the supramolecular structure.\nSupplementary Materials: The following are available online at http://www.mdpi.com/2073-4360/12/12/2912/s1,\nFigure S1: XRD ﬁtting results of softwood ﬁbers: (a) 0, (b) 4000, (c) 8000, (d) 12,000, (e) 16,000 revolutions of PFI\nreﬁning, Figure S2: XRD ﬁtting results of hardwood ﬁbers: (a) 0, (b) 4000, (c) 8000, (d) 12,000, (e) 16,000 revolutions\nof PFI reﬁning, Figure S3: Nonlinear ﬁtting curves of the band of hardwood ﬁbers for hydroxyl groups: (a) 0, (b)\n4000, (c) 8000, (d) 12,000, (e) 16,000 revolutions of PFI reﬁning, Figure S4: The BET N2 adsorption/desorption\nisotherms at various reﬁning revolutions of pulp ﬁbers: (a) softwood; (b) hardwood, Table S1: Cumulative pore\nvolume, average pore size and speciﬁc surface area of softwood pulp ﬁber through reﬁning, Cumulative pore\nvolume, average pore size and speciﬁc surface area of hardwood pulp ﬁber through reﬁning.\n\nAuthor Contributions: Conceptualization, methodology, software, validation, formal analysis, investigation,\ndata curation, writing—original draft preparation, and visualization: K.L.; conceptualization, validation, funding\nacquisition, writing—review and editing: L.Z.; conceptualization, resources, supervision, project administration,\nand funding acquisition: B.H. MinerU85块＋全部既有优化 · 要点 3/3；边界 2/2

CI-XI的值明显高于CI-XA，作者推测这可能与CI-XA分析中无定形贡献过拟合有关。 [1]
例如未精磨时，软木浆的CI-XI为73.23%、CI-XA为40.46%，硬木浆分别为75.55%和47.16%。 [2]
软木浆的CI-XI与CI-XA显著相关，相关系数为0.919（p<0.05）。 [1]
硬木浆的CI-XI与CI-XA显著相关，相关系数为0.925（p<0.05）。 [1]

Methods > 2.4. XRD Analysis\n[原文]\nThe crystallinity of pretreated fibers was determined by a Shimadzu XRD 7000S (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan), while using Cu-Ka radiation. The samples were scanned at 40 kV and 30 mA in a 2θ range of $4 { - } 4 0 ^ { \\circ }$ at 1<sup>◦</sup>/min. It is well known that two polymorphs, cellulose Iα and Iβ, are present in native cellulose; for clarity, all of the reflections indexed here are on the Iβ lattice. Before analysis, the experimental data is nine point smoothed with Savitzky–Golay algorithm. The two types of CI values were obtained from peak intensity method (CI − XI) and peak fitting (CI-XA), respectively. The CI − XI was calculated as in Equation (2) [19].\n\n$$\nC I - X I = \\frac {\\left(I _ {2 0 0} - I _ {a m}\\right)}{I _ {2 0 0}} \\times 1 0 0 \\%\\tag{2}\n$$\n\nwhere I200 is the maximum difraction intensity value of the (200) lattice plane between the scattering angles of $2 \\Theta = 2 2 ^ { \\circ }$ and $2 3 ^ { \\circ }$ , and $I _ { a m }$ is the minimum difraction intensity of amorphous fraction between $2 \\Theta = 1 8 ^ { \\circ }$ and $1 9 ^ { \\circ }$\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 2. Methods > 2.4. XRD Analysis\n[原文]\nAll of the XRD difractograms were smoothed with the Savitzky–Golay algorithm and baseline-corrected with linear fit function. Subsequently, the baseline-corrected difractograms were deconvoluted with the Pearson VII function. The value of the CI-XA equals the area percentage occupied by crystalline peaks over the total area of the difraction pattern [20]. In addition, the crystallite size was calculated by the widely used Scherrer Equation (3) [21]:\n\n$$\nL = \\frac {k \\times \\lambda}{(\\beta \\times \\cos \\theta)}\\tag{3}\n$$\n\nwhere L is the size that is perpendicular to the lattice plane, k is a constant that depends on the crystal shape (0.89), λ is the wavelength of the incident beam in the difraction experiment (0.154 nm), $\\beta$ is the full width at half maximum of the difraction peak, and θ is the Bragg’s angle. In general, the values of the calculated crystallite sizes might be lower than that of the real crystallite sizes, because the peak broadening from the instrumental factors was not considered [22].",

Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\nAs to the free OH(2) and OH(6) of softwood fiber, the relative content showed a slight increase trend in general. The enhancement of the free OH(2) and OH(6) was understandable, because there was the breakage of H-bonds among cellulosic molecules, which resulted in more extensive delamination and higher specific surface area (as shown in Figure S4 and Table S1 in Online Resource). This made cellulose more accessible to water and chemicals. However, for the free OH(2) and OH(6) of hardwood fiber, the number of the free OH(2) and OH(6) decreased by 21.65% from 14.32% to 11.22%, with revolutions increasing from 0 r to 4000 r, followed by an increase of 45.37% in the stage of refining from 4000 r to 12,000 r, along with an decrease of 17.11%. It could be explained by the instability of free OH groups, which makes it easy to form new H-bonds, such as O(2)H···O(6) or O(6)H···O(3′)H-bonds. Thus although there is the formation of free OH(2) and OH(6) during fibrillation, the content of the free OH(2) and OH(6) might disease; meanwhile, the content of the O(6)H···O(3′) or the O(2)H···O(6) H-bonds might increase upon drying.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.4. It was 0.912 (p < 0.05) for softwood fibers and 0.889 (p < 0.05) for hardwood fibers, respectively. Correlation between CI and Content of Inter-Molecular H-Bonds during PFI Refining\n[原文]\nFigure 9. The illustration of a two-phase structure of cellulose.",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 4. Conclusions\n[原文]\nThe results indicated that the fibrillation and properties of fibers are related to the variation of the supramolecular structure during PFI refining. It is noticeable that there was a significantly positive correlation between the CI-XI and content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds during PFI refining for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers. Thus, the trend of the content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds might be generally speculated based on CI-XI while refining. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nRecently, researches indicated that plant cell walls commonly contained microfibrils with 18 cellulose chains [26]. Frequently adopted arrangements of the 18 cellulose chains are 234432, 34443, and 333333 [27]. Therein, 234432 arrangement was found to be more probable based on calculation [28]. Thus, according to the crystallite sizes (as Table 1 shows) and the unit cell parameters of cellulose Iβ, there was most likely to be an average of two-fibrils with an arrangement of 234,432 packed side-by-side for both softwood fibers and hardwood fibers (as seen in Figure 5, drawn with mercury\n\n4.1.2 software). PyMuPDF结构81块基线 · 要点 4/4；边界 2/2

在PFI打浆中，软木纤维和硬木纤维的CI（CI-XI和CI-XA）均表现为先下降、再上升、随后下降。 [3]
这种结晶度波动可能是因为PFI打浆的机械作用作用于纤维素的不同区域。 [3]
第一阶段CI下降表明机械处理可能主要作用于结晶区。 [3]
随后CI上升可解释为更大的作用力作用于非晶区，并在PFI打浆的机械与热作用及干燥过程中可能发生共结晶。 [3]
后续CI下降则可能是结晶区被持续破坏。 [3]
与CI变化相对应，O(6)H···O(3')氢键含量也呈先下降、再上升、随后下降，且结晶区中该氢键含量高于非晶区。 [6]
CI-XI与O(6)H···O(3')氢键含量显著正相关，软木纤维为0.912、硬木纤维为0.889（p<0.05），表明氢键网络变化与结晶度波动相一致。 [6]

  "answer": "在PFI打浆中，软木纤维和硬木纤维的CI（CI-XI和CI-XA）均表现为先下降、再上升、随后下降。 [3]\n这种结晶度波动可能是因为PFI打浆的机械作用作用于纤维素的不同区域。 [3]\n第一阶段CI下降表明机械处理可能主要作用于结晶区。 [3]\n随后CI上升可解释为更大的作用力作用于非晶区，并在PFI打浆的机械与热作用及干燥过程中可能发生共结晶。 [3]\n后续CI下降则可能是结晶区被持续破坏。 [3]\n与CI变化相对应，O(6)H···O(3')氢键含量也呈先下降、再上升、随后下降，且结晶区中该氢键含量高于非晶区。 [6]\nCI-XI与O(6)H···O(3')氢键含量显著正相关，软木纤维为0.912、硬木纤维为0.889（p<0.05），表明氢键网络变化与结晶度波动相一致。 [6]",

      "text": "In the case of the O(2)H· · · O(6) intra-molecular H-bonds for softwood ﬁber, the trend of content\ncan be described as two phases. It had an increase of 3.5% from 31.4% to 32.5% in the stage of reﬁning\nfrom 0 r to 4000 r and it then decreased by 21.57% from 4000 r to 12000 r, along with a growth of 15.26%\nin the last reﬁning stage. For the content of the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds of hardwood ﬁber, it increased\nﬁrstly and then had a decrease that was also followed by an increase. For both ﬁbers, the content of\nO(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds decreased, except for the stage of reﬁning from 0 r to 4000 r. It might be due to\nthe fact that the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds, which are much more accessible to water, are less stable than\nO(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds.\nAs to the free OH(2) and OH(6) of softwood fiber, the relative content showed a slight increase trend\nin general. The enhancement of the free OH(2) and OH(6) was understandable, because there was the\nbreakage of H-bonds among cellulosic molecules, which resulted in more extensive delamination and\nhigher specific surface area (as shown in Figure S4 and Table S1 in Online Resource). This made cellulose\nmore accessible to water and chemicals. However, for the free OH(2) and OH(6) of hardwood fiber,\nthe number of the free OH(2) and OH(6) decreased by 21.65% from 14.32% to 11.22%, with revolutions\nincreasing from 0 r to 4000 r, followed by an increase of 45.37% in the stage of refining from 4000 r to\n12,000 r, along with an decrease of 17.11%. It could be explained by the instability of free OH groups,\nwhich makes it easy to form new H-bonds, such as O(2)H···O(6) or O(6)H···O(3′)H-bonds. Thus although\nthere is the formation of free OH(2) and OH(6) during fibrillation, the content of the free OH(2) and OH(6)\nmight disease; meanwhile, the content of the O(6)H···O(3′) or the O(2)H···O(6) H-bonds might increase\nupon drying.\n\n3.4. Correlation between CI and Content of Inter-Molecular H-Bonds during PFI Reﬁning\nSimilar to the CI-XI, the content of O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds decreased ﬁrst and then had an increase,\nfollowed by a decline for the two ﬁbers (as shown in Figure 8a,b). Besides, the Pearson correlation\ncoeﬃcients were calculated between the content of H-bonds and the CI-XI. It was 0.912 (p < 0.05)\nfor softwood ﬁbers and 0.889 (p < 0.05) for hardwood ﬁbers, respectively.       "Polymers 2020, 12, 2912 12 of 14\nThe results indicated that the ﬁbrillation and properties of ﬁbers are related to the variation of the\nsupramolecular structure during PFI reﬁning. It is noticeable that there was a signiﬁcantly positive\ncorrelation between the CI-XI and content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds during PFI reﬁning for softwood\nﬁbers and hardwood ﬁbers. Thus, the trend of the content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds might be generally\nspeculated based on CI-XI while reﬁning. Besides, the crystallite size, crystallinity, and content of\nvarious H-bonds did not change much in general. It is assumed that PFI reﬁning is an excellent\nmechanical treatment of ﬁbrillation with relatively little destruction on the supramolecular structure.\nSupplementary Materials: The following are available online at http://www.mdpi.com/2073-4360/12/12/2912/s1,\nFigure S1: XRD ﬁtting results of softwood ﬁbers: (a) 0, (b) 4000, (c) 8000, (d) 12,000, (e) 16,000 revolutions of PFI\nreﬁning, Figure S2: XRD ﬁtting results of hardwood ﬁbers: (a) 0, (b) 4000, (c) 8000, (d) 12,000, (e) 16,000 revolutions\nof PFI reﬁning, Figure S3: Nonlinear ﬁtting curves of the band of hardwood ﬁbers for hydroxyl groups: (a) 0, (b)\n4000, (c) 8000, (d) 12,000, (e) 16,000 revolutions of PFI reﬁning, Figure S4: The BET N2 adsorption/desorption\nisotherms at various reﬁning revolutions of pulp ﬁbers: (a) softwood; (b) hardwood, Table S1: Cumulative pore\nvolume, average pore size and speciﬁc surface area of softwood pulp ﬁber through reﬁning, Cumulative pore\nvolume, average pore size and speciﬁc surface area of hardwood pulp ﬁber through reﬁning.\n\nAuthor Contributions: Conceptualization, methodology, software, validation, formal analysis, investigation,\ndata curation, writing—original draft preparation, and visualization: K.L.; conceptualization, validation, funding\nacquisition, writing—review and editing: L.Z.; conceptualization, resources, supervision, project administration,\nand funding acquisition: B.H.       "Polymers 2020, 12, 2912 2 of 14\nﬁrst and then decreased with the degree of reﬁning for hardwood bleached kraft pulp ﬁbers [11] or\nfor unbleached eucalyptus ﬁbers [12]. Moreover, Zhao et al. [7] reported that the crystallinity initially\nﬂuctuated upward and then downward, followed by a repeating ﬂuctuation with PFI reﬁning for\ntobacco stem mechanical pulp. None of the previous studies identiﬁed a clear trend, but the results\nwere that the crystallinity varied during PFI reﬁnement. Based on the large proportion of H-bonds in\ncrystalline region of cellulose, it can be assumed that the H-bonding network might change during\nPFI reﬁning.\nFourier transformation infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), which is sensitive to molecular structure,\ncan be as an indirect measurement for studying H-bonding network. FT-IR deconvolution of hydroxyl\ngroups band was adopted in order to study the changes of the energy of H-bonds and the H-bonding\ndistance during deligniﬁcation [13] or the deconstruction of cellulose [14]. Moreover, it was used\nto study the diﬀerences of the content of H-bonds not only between dislocation region and normal\nregion [15], but also among plant species [16,17]. Regarding the changes of H-bonding network during\nPFI reﬁning, Yuan et al. [18] reported that the content of H-bonds and crystallinity index (CI) of\neucalyptus ﬁbers changed with the increment of beating time. Subsequently, Zhao et al. [8] found that\nthe H-bonding energy for O(6)H· · · O(3′) inter-molecular H-bonds decreased by 12.9% and evolutions\nof the content of certain H-bonds diﬀered at various reﬁning stages.\n\nThere is still a lack of literature on the eﬀects of PFI reﬁnement on the H-bonding network.\nParticularly, the relationship between the content of H-bonds and crystallinity is still worthy of\nfurther study, which will deepen the understanding of the molecular aggregation and distribution of\nH-bonds, providing a molecular-scale explanation for the variations in accessibility, swelling, ﬂexibility,\nand ﬁbrillation of cellulosic ﬁbers during PFI reﬁnement. Therefore, this work explored the eﬀects\nof PFI reﬁnement on the CI, crystallite size, energy of H-bonds, H-bonding distance, and content of\nH-bonds for softwood pulp ﬁbers and hardwood pulp ﬁbers. Attempts were made in order to establish\nthe correlations between the CI and content of various H-bonds.",

      "Keywords: natural cellulosic ﬁbers; mechanical reﬁning; Crystallinity; Crystallite size;\nHydrogen bonds\n\n1. Introduction\nMechanical, chemical, and biological treatments are usually adopted to obtain the desired\nphysical and mechanical properties and for further utilization of the natural cellulosic ﬁbers. Therein,\nPapirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) reﬁning is the most common laboratory reﬁner in order to\nimprove the inter-ﬁber bonding capacity [1] and accessibility [2,3], and manufacture the micro-ﬁbrillated\nor nano-ﬁbrillated cellulose [4–6]. The main eﬀects of PFI reﬁning on ﬁbers are: (i) internal\nﬁbrillation—delaminating, loosening, and swelling of ﬁber wall; (ii) external ﬁbrillation—peeling of\nﬁbrils from the ﬁber surface while remaining attached; (iii) ﬁber shortening—ﬁber cutting due to\nshearing action, and (iv) ﬁnes formation—primary ﬁnes come from ray cells and parenchyma cells\nand microﬁbrils that are caused by ﬁber shortening or external ﬁbrillation. Moreover, the PFI reﬁning\ncould be adopted to obtain a higher internal ﬁbrillation than other laboratory reﬁners [1]. These eﬀects\nof the PFI reﬁning on cellulosic ﬁbers will improve the accessibility, the swelling, the ﬂexibility, and the\ninter-ﬁber bonding capacity of ﬁbers. It is assumed that these changes in the macro-level structure and\nproperties are related to the changes of crystallinity and H-bonding network during reﬁning [7,8].\n\nThere are some diﬀerent conclusions regarding to the eﬀects of PFI reﬁning on crystallinity of\ncellulose, not like that of ball milling, which eﬀectively reduces the crystallinity as the treatment\nprogresses. Although some researchers considered that the crystallinity decreased during PFI reﬁning\nfor corn stover [9] or softwood pulp [10], some researchers reported that the crystallinity increased\nPolymers 2020, 12, 2912; doi:10.3390/polym12122912 www.mdpi.com/journal/polymers",
      "3.1. The Morphological Analysis, Swelling, and Mechanical Properties\nFor softwood ﬁbers and hardwood ﬁbers, the macro-ﬁbrillation index and the ﬁber length had\na downward trend, and the ﬁnes content has an upward trend for the softwood ﬁbers during PFI\nreﬁning, as can be seen in Figure 1. The macro-ﬁbrillation index and ﬁber length of softwood ﬁbers\nchanged signiﬁcantly. However, two parameters of hardwood ﬁbers had no signiﬁcant variations\nrelative to softwood ﬁbers. It might be because of the lower reﬁning pressure that was applied in\nhardwood ﬁbers. The macro-ﬁbrillation index characterizes external macro-ﬁbrillation. The results of\nﬁber morphology analysis showed that external ﬁbrillation increased with the reﬁning process. It is\nconsistent with the increasing speciﬁc surface area (as shown in Table S1 in Online Resource).\n\nFigure 1. The morphological analysis for the unreﬁned and reﬁned samples: (a) softwood ﬁbers and\n(b) hardwood ﬁbers.\nThe beating degree and the WRV had a signiﬁcant increment with increasing PFI reﬁning\nrevolutions, as can be seen in Figure 2. It is caused by the higher ﬁbrillation that produces the\nnew surface and more pores (as shown in Table S1 in Online Resource). The increase in swelling\ncharacterized by WRV makes the ﬁbers more compliant in transverse [1], which contributes to\nimproving the inter-ﬁber bonding strength of the ﬁber network. The results of ﬁber morphology\nanalysis and water retention value showing that the ﬁbrillation and the separation between ﬁbrils\nincrease with the reﬁning process.",

      "2. Methods\n\n2.1. PFI Reﬁning\nCommercial bleached softwood and hardwood kraft pulp ﬁbers were obtained from\nZhongzhirenhe Company (Jinan, Shandong Province, China). Two pulp were treated with a PFI reﬁner\n(Hamjern Maskin A/S, Hamar, Norway) according to Tappi T248 wd-97, with a pulp consistency\nof 10%, the gap between the opposite reﬁning plates was 0.2 mm, and forces per bar length were\n3.33 N/mm and 1.77 N/mm for softwood ﬁbers and hardwood ﬁbers, respectively. The drainability was\ncharacterized by the Schopper Riegler number (SR-number) with the standards ISO 5267-1. Two pulp\nﬁbers were separately reﬁned in a PFI reﬁner at 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions and\nat 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions, respectively. Corresponding various pulps with an\nincreasing beating degree, such as 16, 20, 40, 63, and 79◦SR, were obtained for softwood ﬁbers and 0,\n26, 40, 57, and 70◦SR were obtained for hardwood ﬁbers.\n\n2.2. Morphological Analysis of Fibers and Mechanical Properties of Sheets\nThe ﬁnes content, weighted mean length, and macro-ﬁbrillation index of each sample were\ndetermined with a MORFI LB analyzer (Techpap SAS, Grenoble, France). The tensile strength of\ndry sheets and Wet-web strength were tested according to TAPPI T494 and Chinese standard GBT\n12914-2008, respectively. The zero-span tensile strength was tested with the Z-Span 2400 apparatus\n(Pulmac International Co. Ltd., Montpelier, VT, USA), according to the standard ISO 15361."

在该研究的软木浆和硬木浆中，CI-XI和CI-XA随PFI打浆（0–16000转）均表现为先下降、再上升、随后下降。 [2]
作者解释第一阶段结晶度下降是因为PFI机械处理主要作用于结晶区。 [2]
随后结晶度上升被解释为机械力更多作用于无定形区，并可能在PFI的机械和热作用下于干燥时发生共结晶。 [2]
最后的下降可能源于结晶区被持续破坏。 [2]
O(6)H···O(3′)分子间氢键含量也呈先降、后升、再降，且与CI-XI显著相关（软木r=0.912，硬木r=0.889，p<0.05）。 [3]
这种相关性的解释是结晶区比无定形区含有更高含量的O(6)H···O(3′)氢键。 [3]
这些摘录指出既往关于PFI打浆对结晶度影响的结论并不一致，且未识别出明确趋势，因此上述机制是该研究对软木和硬木浆结果的解释，不能据此认定适用于其他原料或打浆条件。 [1]

      "text": "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\nMechanical, chemical, and biological treatments are usually adopted to obtain the desired physical and mechanical properties and for further utilization of the natural cellulosic fibers. Therein, Papirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) refining is the most common laboratory refiner in order to improve the inter-fiber bonding capacity [1] and accessibility [2,3], and manufacture the micro-fibrillated or nano-fibrillated cellulose [4–6]. The main efects of PFI refining on fibers are: (i) internal fibrillation—delaminating, loosening, and swelling of fiber wall; (ii) external fibrillation—peeling of fibrils from the fiber surface while remaining attached; (iii) fiber shortening—fiber cutting due to shearing action, and (iv) fines formation—primary fines come from ray cells and parenchyma cells and microfibrils that are caused by fiber shortening or external fibrillation. Moreover, the PFI refining could be adopted to obtain a higher internal fibrillation than other laboratory refiners [1]. These efects of the PFI refining on cellulosic fibers will improve the accessibility, the swelling, the flexibility, and the inter-fiber bonding capacity of fibers.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\n It is assumed that these changes in the macro-level structure and properties are related to the changes of crystallinity and H-bonding network during refining [7,8].\n\nThere are some diferent conclusions regarding to the efects of PFI refining on crystallinity of cellulose, not like that of ball milling, which efectively reduces the crystallinity as the treatment progresses. Although some researchers considered that the crystallinity decreased during PFI refining for corn stover [9] or softwood pulp [10], some researchers reported that the crystallinity increased first and then decreased with the degree of refining for hardwood bleached kraft pulp fibers [11] or for unbleached eucalyptus fibers [12]. Moreover, Zhao et al. [7] reported that the crystallinity initially fluctuated upward and then downward, followed by a repeating fluctuation with PFI refining for tobacco stem mechanical pulp. None of the previous studies identified a clear trend, but the results were that the crystallinity varied during PFI refinement. Based on the large proportion of H-bonds in crystalline region of cellulose, it can be assumed that the H-bonding network might change during PFI refining.",

Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\nAs to the free OH(2) and OH(6) of softwood fiber, the relative content showed a slight increase trend in general. The enhancement of the free OH(2) and OH(6) was understandable, because there was the breakage of H-bonds among cellulosic molecules, which resulted in more extensive delamination and higher specific surface area (as shown in Figure S4 and Table S1 in Online Resource). This made cellulose more accessible to water and chemicals. However, for the free OH(2) and OH(6) of hardwood fiber, the number of the free OH(2) and OH(6) decreased by 21.65% from 14.32% to 11.22%, with revolutions increasing from 0 r to 4000 r, followed by an increase of 45.37% in the stage of refining from 4000 r to 12,000 r, along with an decrease of 17.11%. It could be explained by the instability of free OH groups, which makes it easy to form new H-bonds, such as O(2)H···O(6) or O(6)H···O(3′)H-bonds.       "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\nMechanical, chemical, and biological treatments are usually adopted to obtain the desired physical and mechanical properties and for further utilization of the natural cellulosic fibers. Therein, Papirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) refining is the most common laboratory refiner in order to improve the inter-fiber bonding capacity [1] and accessibility [2,3], and manufacture the micro-fibrillated or nano-fibrillated cellulose [4–6]. The main efects of PFI refining on fibers are: (i) internal fibrillation—delaminating, loosening, and swelling of fiber wall; (ii) external fibrillation—peeling of fibrils from the fiber surface while remaining attached; (iii) fiber shortening—fiber cutting due to shearing action, and (iv) fines formation—primary fines come from ray cells and parenchyma cells and microfibrils that are caused by fiber shortening or external fibrillation. Moreover, the PFI refining could be adopted to obtain a higher internal fibrillation than other laboratory refiners [1]. These efects of the PFI refining on cellulosic fibers will improve the accessibility, the swelling, the flexibility, and the inter-fiber bonding capacity of fibers.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\n It is assumed that these changes in the macro-level structure and properties are related to the changes of crystallinity and H-bonding network during refining [7,8].\n\nThere are some diferent conclusions regarding to the efects of PFI refining on crystallinity of cellulose, not like that of ball milling, which efectively reduces the crystallinity as the treatment progresses. Although some researchers considered that the crystallinity decreased during PFI refining for corn stover [9] or softwood pulp [10], some researchers reported that the crystallinity increased first and then decreased with the degree of refining for hardwood bleached kraft pulp fibers [11] or for unbleached eucalyptus fibers [12]. Moreover, Zhao et al. [7] reported that the crystallinity initially fluctuated upward and then downward, followed by a repeating fluctuation with PFI refining for tobacco stem mechanical pulp. None of the previous studies identified a clear trend, but the results were that the crystallinity varied during PFI refinement. Based on the large proportion of H-bonds in crystalline region of cellulose, it can be assumed that the H-bonding network might change during PFI refining.",

Results and Discussions > 3.2. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nThe trends of CI (CI-XI and CI-XA) for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers were all similar, decreasing first and then increasing, along with a decline, as shown in Figure 4. The fluctuation of the CI was probably because of the mechanical action of PFI refining on the diferent regions of cellulose. In the first refining stage, the decrease of the CI showed that mechanical treatment may mainly act in the crystalline region. Subsequently, the growth of the CI could be interpreted as greater force acting on the amorphous region in which cocrystallization might occur upon drying under the mechanical and thermal action of PFI refining. The subsequent decrease might be the continuous destruction of crystalline region.",

The enhancement of the free OH(2) and OH(6) was understandable, because there was the breakage of H-bonds among cellulosic molecules, which resulted in more extensive delamination and higher specific surface area (as shown in Figure S4 and Table S1 in Online Resource). It could be explained by the instability of free OH groups, which makes it easy to form new H-bonds, such as O(2)H···O(6) or O(6)H···O(3′)H-bonds. Thus although there is the formation of free OH(2) and OH(6) during fibrillation, the content of the free OH(2) and OH(6) might disease; meanwhile, the content of the O(6)H···O(3′) or the O(2)H···O(6) H-bonds might increase upon drying.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nIt is known that both the (1\\overline{1}0) and the (110) lattice plane are hydrophilic, and the (200)lattice plane is hydrophobic in cellulose Iβ (as Figure 5 shows). In addition, it is noticeable that the (110) planes possess the highest theoretical roughness and accessibility to the hydrophilic groups in cellulose Iβ [28]. Throughout the refining of two pulp fibers, the sizes perpendicular to (110) plane were more volatile than the (1\\overline{1}0) plane and (200) plane, which is consistent with the report of Duchemin et al., as shown in Table 1a,b [29]. It could be interpreted to be that water molecules were easier to permeate through the spaces between the hydrophilic (110) planes in paracrystalline region (hydration), and then it made these planes suffer more mechanical actions, so there was more adhesion (cocrystallization) and cleavage of cellulose chains created for (110) plane during PFI refining.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.2. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nHowever, the crystallite size that was perpendicular to (200) lattice plane of two fibers had an upward trend during PFI refining. It could be explained in terms of coalescence of chains or some crystallographic stacking of adjacent microfibrils, where the (200) planes were aligned upon drying [30]. Additionally, it was probably due to the weaker cleavage effect on (200) lattice planes that was hard for water molecules to penetrate.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.3. Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\nAs to the O(3)H· · · O(5) intra-molecular H-bonds of softwood fiber, the content had a growth of 10.09% from 28.44% to 31.31% in the stage of refining from 0 r to 4000 r, and then had a slight decrease of 1.44% from 4000 r to 8000 r, followed by an increase of 13.16% until the end of refining. Overall, the trend was similar to that of hardwood fibers, which first increased and then had a decrease, followed by a growth. During the whole refining, the amount of $\\mathrm { O } ( 3 ) \\mathrm { H } \\cdots \\mathrm { O } ( 5 )$ H-bonds for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers showed an upward tendency and increased by 22.78% and 8.8%, respectively. The increase might be because the stable O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds might have not only less breakage under the action of water as destructor to the crystallites [30], but also creation in the amorphous region upon drying. Because hydrogen bond–covalent bond synergies play an important role in the cellulose stifness axial modulus, more O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds will enhance the cellulose stifness [33,34].\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.3. For the content of the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds of hardwood fiber, it increased firstly and then had a decrease that was also followed by an increase. Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nThe cellulose polymorph of these two fibers had no change during PFI treatment, which illustrates that the PFI refining is a relatively mild mechanical treatment, as the results of XRD in Online Resource (Figures S1 and S2) show. Frequently adopted arrangements of the 18 cellulose chains are 234432, 34443, and 333333 [27]. Therein, 234432 arrangement was found to be more probable based on calculation [28]. Thus, according to the crystallite sizes (as Table 1 shows) and the unit cell parameters of cellulose Iβ, there was most likely to be an average of two-fibrils with an arrangement of 234,432 packed side-by-side for both softwood fibers and hardwood fibers (as seen in Figure 5, drawn with mercury\n\n4.1.2 software). The result is consistent with the report of Haigler & Roberts [26], which shows that there might be two microfibrils associated along part of their length."

PyMuPDF结构81块基线 · 要点 2/2；边界 2/2

PFI打浆回合数增加时，打浆度和WRV显著提高，作者将其归因于更高程度的细纤维化产生新表面和更多孔隙。 [1]
以WRV表征的润胀增加使纤维在横向上更柔顺，这有助于提高纤维网络的纤维间结合强度。 [1]
PFI打浆的主要效应包括内细纤维化使纤维壁分层、松散和润胀，以及外细纤维化等，并改善纤维的可及性、润胀、柔顺性和纤维间结合能力。 [2]
PFI打浆提高了细纤维化程度（尤其是内细纤维化）和纤维润胀，且不降低纤维强度，从而提高纸页抗张强度。 [3]

  "answer": "PFI打浆回合数增加时，打浆度和WRV显著提高，作者将其归因于更高程度的细纤维化产生新表面和更多孔隙。 [1]\n以WRV表征的润胀增加使纤维在横向上更柔顺，这有助于提高纤维网络的纤维间结合强度。 [1]\nPFI打浆的主要效应包括内细纤维化使纤维壁分层、松散和润胀，以及外细纤维化等，并改善纤维的可及性、润胀、柔顺性和纤维间结合能力。 [2]\nPFI打浆提高了细纤维化程度（尤其是内细纤维化）和纤维润胀，且不降低纤维强度，从而提高纸页抗张强度。 [3]",

      "text": "polymers\nArticle\nProbing Eﬀect of Papirindustriens Forskningsinstitut\n(PFI) Reﬁning on Aggregation Structure of Cellulose:\nCrystal Packing and Hydrogen-Bonding Network\nKunpeng Li, Lihong Zhao * and Beihai He\nState Key Laboratory of Pulp and Paper Engineering, South China University of Technology, 381 Wushan Rd.,\nTianhe District, Guangzhou 510640, China; felikp@mail.scut.edu.cn (K.L.); ppebhhe@scut.edu.cn (B.H.)\n* Correspondence: zhaolh@scut.edu.cn\nReceived: 17 November 2020; Accepted: 2 December 2020; Published: 4 December 2020\nAbstract: Supramolecular structure is the critical factor that aﬀects the properties of cellulosic\nﬁbers. This article studied the action of Papirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) reﬁning on the\nmolecular aggregation and hydrogen bonding network, and tried to explore the relationship between\nthe crystal packing and hydrogen-bonding network in cellulosic ﬁbers. The results showed that\nthe polymorph, H-bonding distance, and H-bonding energy of various H-bonds remained almost\nunchanged, while the crystalline index, crystallite size, and content of various H-bonds changed\nwith reﬁning. Therein, the content of the inter-molecular O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds was signiﬁcantly\ncorrelated with the crystalline index that was obtained in intensities of the XRD peaks. The Pearson\ncorrelation coeﬃcient between them was 0.888 (p < 0.05) for softwood ﬁbers and 0.889 (p < 0.05)\nfor hardwood ﬁbers, respectively. It can be concluded that the variations of accessibility, swelling,\nand ﬁbrillation were closely related to the supramolecular structure and the intermolecular H-bonds\nplay an important role in the crystal packing of cellulose.\n\nKeywords: natural cellulosic ﬁbers; mechanical reﬁning; Crystallinity; Crystallite size;\nHydrogen bonds\n\n1. Introduction\nMechanical, chemical, and biological treatments are usually adopted to obtain the desired\nphysical and mechanical properties and for further utilization of the natural cellulosic ﬁbers. Therein,\nPapirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) reﬁning is the most common laboratory reﬁner in order to\nimprove the inter-ﬁber bonding capacity [1] and accessibility [2,3], and manufacture the micro-ﬁbrillated\nor nano-ﬁbrillated cellulose [4–6]. The main eﬀects of PFI reﬁning on ﬁbers are: (i) internal\nﬁbrillation—delaminating, loosening, and swelling of ﬁber wall; (ii) external ﬁbrillation—peeling of\nﬁbrils from the ﬁber surface while remaining attached; (iii) ﬁber shortening—ﬁber cutting due to\nshearing action, and (iv) ﬁnes formation—primary ﬁnes come from ray cells and parenchyma cells\nand microﬁbrils that are caused by ﬁber shortening or external ﬁbrillation. Moreover, the PFI reﬁning\ncould be adopted to obtain a higher internal ﬁbrillation than other laboratory reﬁners [1]. These eﬀects\nof the PFI reﬁning on cellulosic ﬁbers will improve the accessibility, the swelling, the ﬂexibility, and the\ninter-ﬁber bonding capacity of ﬁbers. It is assumed that these changes in the macro-level structure and\nproperties are related to the changes of crystallinity and H-bonding network during reﬁning [7,8].\n\nThere are some diﬀerent conclusions regarding to the eﬀects of PFI reﬁning on crystallinity of\ncellulose, not like that of ball milling, which eﬀectively reduces the crystallinity as the treatment\nprogresses.       "Polymers 2020, 12, 2912 2 of 14\nﬁrst and then decreased with the degree of reﬁning for hardwood bleached kraft pulp ﬁbers [11] or\nfor unbleached eucalyptus ﬁbers [12]. Moreover, Zhao et al. [7] reported that the crystallinity initially\nﬂuctuated upward and then downward, followed by a repeating ﬂuctuation with PFI reﬁning for\ntobacco stem mechanical pulp. None of the previous studies identiﬁed a clear trend, but the results\nwere that the crystallinity varied during PFI reﬁnement. Based on the large proportion of H-bonds in\ncrystalline region of cellulose, it can be assumed that the H-bonding network might change during\nPFI reﬁning.\nFourier transformation infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), which is sensitive to molecular structure,\ncan be as an indirect measurement for studying H-bonding network. FT-IR deconvolution of hydroxyl\ngroups band was adopted in order to study the changes of the energy of H-bonds and the H-bonding\ndistance during deligniﬁcation [13] or the deconstruction of cellulose [14]. Moreover, it was used\nto study the diﬀerences of the content of H-bonds not only between dislocation region and normal\nregion [15], but also among plant species [16,17]. Regarding the changes of H-bonding network during\nPFI reﬁning, Yuan et al. [18] reported that the content of H-bonds and crystallinity index (CI) of\neucalyptus ﬁbers changed with the increment of beating time. Subsequently, Zhao et al. [8] found that\nthe H-bonding energy for O(6)H· · · O(3′) inter-molecular H-bonds decreased by 12.9% and evolutions\nof the content of certain H-bonds diﬀered at various reﬁning stages.\n\nThere is still a lack of literature on the eﬀects of PFI reﬁnement on the H-bonding network.\nParticularly, the relationship between the content of H-bonds and crystallinity is still worthy of\nfurther study, which will deepen the understanding of the molecular aggregation and distribution of\nH-bonds, providing a molecular-scale explanation for the variations in accessibility, swelling, ﬂexibility,\nand ﬁbrillation of cellulosic ﬁbers during PFI reﬁnement. Therefore, this work explored the eﬀects\nof PFI reﬁnement on the CI, crystallite size, energy of H-bonds, H-bonding distance, and content of\nH-bonds for softwood pulp ﬁbers and hardwood pulp ﬁbers. Attempts were made in order to establish\nthe correlations between the CI and content of various H-bonds.\n\n2. Methods",

      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 未确定\n[原文]\nKunpeng Li, Lihong Zhao \\* and Beihai He\n\nState Key Laboratory of Pulp and Paper Engineering, South China University of Technology, 381 Wushan Rd., Tianhe District, Guangzhou 510640, China; felikp@mail.scut.edu.cn (K.L.); ppebhhe@scut.edu.cn (B.H.) \\* Correspondence: zhaolh@scut.edu.cn\n\nReceived: 17 November 2020; Accepted: 2 December 2020; Published: 4 December 2020\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 未确定\n[原文]\nAbstract: Supramolecular structure is the critical factor that affects the properties of cellulosic fibers. This article studied the action of Papirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) refining on the molecular aggregation and hydrogen bonding network, and tried to explore the relationship between the crystal packing and hydrogen-bonding network in cellulosic fibers. The results showed that the polymorph, H-bonding distance, and H-bonding energy of various H-bonds remained almost unchanged, while the crystalline index, crystallite size, and content of various H-bonds changed with refining. Therein, the content of the inter-molecular O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds was significantly correlated with the crystalline index that was obtained in intensities of the XRD peaks. The Pearson correlation coefficient between them was 0.888 (p < 0.05) for softwood fibers and 0.889 (p < 0.05) for hardwood fibers, respectively. It can be concluded that the variations of accessibility, swelling, and fibrillation were closely related to the supramolecular structure and the intermolecular H-bonds play an important role in the crystal packing of cellulose.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\nMechanical, chemical, and biological treatments are usually adopted to obtain the desired physical and mechanical properties and for further utilization of the natural cellulosic fibers. Therein, Papirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) refining is the most common laboratory refiner in order to improve the inter-fiber bonding capacity [1] and accessibility [2,3], and manufacture the micro-fibrillated or nano-fibrillated cellulose [4–6]. The main efects of PFI refining on fibers are: (i) internal fibrillation—delaminating, loosening, and swelling of fiber wall; (ii) external fibrillation—peeling of fibrils from the fiber surface while remaining attached; (iii) fiber shortening—fiber cutting due to shearing action, and (iv) fines formation—primary fines come from ray cells and parenchyma cells and microfibrils that are caused by fiber shortening or external fibrillation. Moreover, the PFI refining could be adopted to obtain a higher internal fibrillation than other laboratory refiners [1]. These efects of the PFI refining on cellulosic fibers will improve the accessibility, the swelling, the flexibility, and the inter-fiber bonding capacity of fibers.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\n It is assumed that these changes in the macro-level structure and properties are related to the changes of crystallinity and H-bonding network during refining [7,8].\n\nThere are some diferent conclusions regarding to the efects of PFI refining on crystallinity of cellulose, not like that of ball milling, which efectively reduces the crystallinity as the treatment progresses. Although some researchers considered that the crystallinity decreased during PFI refining for corn stover [9] or softwood pulp [10], some researchers reported that the crystallinity increased first and then decreased with the degree of refining for hardwood bleached kraft pulp fibers [11] or for unbleached eucalyptus fibers [12]. Moreover, Zhao et al. [7] reported that the crystallinity initially fluctuated upward and then downward, followed by a repeating fluctuation with PFI refining for tobacco stem mechanical pulp. None of the previous studies identified a clear trend, but the results were that the crystallinity varied during PFI refinement. Based on the large proportion of H-bonds in crystalline region of cellulose, it can be assumed that the H-bonding network might change during PFI refining.",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.3. Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\nFor the content of O(6)H···O(3′) inter-molecular H-bonds of softwood fiber, the trend can be divided into two stages, as shown in Table 2a. It decreased by 7.72% from 28.23% to 26.05% as refining from 0r to 4000 r and then increased by 9.14% from 4000 r to 8000 r, followed by a decrease of 17.13%, with the revolutions increasing from 8000 r to 16,000 r. Regarding the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds of hardwood fiber, the trend was almost similar to that of softwood fibers, except for a small increase of 0.45% from 8000 r to 12,000 r (in Table 2b). On the whole, the amount of the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers decreased by 16.54% and 5.91% altogether, respectively. The decrease might be due to the cleavage among cellulose molecular chains under the mechanical action of PFI refining, which was closely related to internal and external fibrillation (as seen in Section 3.1). On the other hand, the increase illustrates that there was not only the breakage, but also the formation of O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.3. Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\n Both the fewer inter-molecular H-bonds and the lower CI (as Section 3.2 shows) will further improve the flexibility of cellulosic fibers, due to the higher mobility of molecular chains, the accessibility, and the WRV of fibers (as seen in Section 3.1).",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.3. Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\nAs to the O(3)H· · · O(5) intra-molecular H-bonds of softwood fiber, the content had a growth of 10.09% from 28.44% to 31.31% in the stage of refining from 0 r to 4000 r, and then had a slight decrease of 1.44% from 4000 r to 8000 r, followed by an increase of 13.16% until the end of refining. Overall, the trend was similar to that of hardwood fibers, which first increased and then had a decrease, followed by a growth. During the whole refining, the amount of $\\mathrm { O } ( 3 ) \\mathrm { H } \\cdots \\mathrm { O } ( 5 )$ H-bonds for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers showed an upward tendency and increased by 22.78% and 8.8%, respectively. The increase might be because the stable O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds might have not only less breakage under the action of water as destructor to the crystallites [30], but also creation in the amorphous region upon drying. Because hydrogen bond–covalent bond synergies play an important role in the cellulose stifness axial modulus, more O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds will enhance the cellulose stifness [33,34].\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.3. Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\nIn the case of the O(2)H· · · O(6) intra-molecular H-bonds for softwood fiber, the trend of content can be described as two phases. It had an increase of 3.5% from 31.4% to 32.5% in the stage of refining from 0 r to 4000 r and it then decreased by 21.57% from 4000 r to 12000 r, along with a growth of 15.26% in the last refining stage. For the content of the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds of hardwood fiber, it increased firstly and then had a decrease that was also followed by an increase. For both fibers, the content of O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds decreased, except for the stage of refining from 0 r to 4000 r. It might be due to the fact that the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds, which are much more accessible to water, are less stable than O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.3. Efect of PFI Refining on H-Bonding Energies, H-Bonding Distances, and Content of H-Bonds\n[原文]\nAs to the free OH(2) and OH(6) of softwood fiber, the relative content showed a slight increase trend in general. The enhancement of the free OH(2) and OH(6) was understandable, because there was the breakage of H-bonds among cellulosic molecules, which resulted in more extensive delamination and higher specific surface area (as shown in Figure S4 and Table S1 in Online Resource). This made cellulose more accessible to water and chemicals. However, for the free OH(2) and OH(6) of hardwood fiber, the number of the free OH(2) and OH(6) decreased by 21.65% from 14.32% to 11.22%, with revolutions increasing from 0 r to 4000 r, followed by an increase of 45.37% in the stage of refining from 4000 r to 12,000 r, along with an decrease of 17.11%. It could be explained by the instability of free OH groups, which makes it easy to form new H-bonds, such as O(2)H···O(6) or O(6)H···O(3′)H-bonds. Thus although there is the formation of free OH(2) and OH(6) during fibrillation, the content of the free OH(2) and OH(6) might disease; meanwhile, the content of the O(6)H···O(3′) or the O(2)H···O(6) H-bonds might increase upon drying.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 3. Results and Discussions > 3.4. Correlation between CI and Content of Inter-Molecular H-Bonds during PFI Refining\n[原文]\nSimilar to the CI-XI, the content of O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds decreased first and then had an increase, followed by a decline for the two fibers (as shown in Figure 8a,b). It was 0.912 (p < 0.05) for softwood fibers and 0.889 (p < 0.05) for hardwood fibers, respectively. PyMuPDF结构81块基线 · 要点 2/3；边界 1/2

打浆（PFI refining）后，针叶木纤维和阔叶木纤维的长度均呈下降趋势。 [1]
针叶木纤维的长度在打浆过程中变化显著，而阔叶木纤维长度的变化相对不显著。 [1]
造成差别的原因可能是阔叶木打浆时所施加的打浆压力较低。 [1]
该研究中PFI打浆对针叶木和阔叶木的每杆长作用力分别为3.33 N/mm和1.77 N/mm，即阔叶木所受打浆作用力较低。 [7]
PFI打浆的主要作用之一是因剪切作用造成的纤维切断，即纤维变短。 [3]

Introduction\nMechanical, chemical, and biological treatments are usually adopted to obtain the desired\nphysical and mechanical properties and for further utilization of the natural cellulosic ﬁbers. Therein,\nPapirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) reﬁning is the most common laboratory reﬁner in order to\nimprove the inter-ﬁber bonding capacity [1] and accessibility [2,3], and manufacture the micro-ﬁbrillated\nor nano-ﬁbrillated cellulose [4–6]. The main eﬀects of PFI reﬁning on ﬁbers are: (i) internal\nﬁbrillation—delaminating, loosening, and swelling of ﬁber wall; (ii) external ﬁbrillation—peeling of\nﬁbrils from the ﬁber surface while remaining attached; (iii) ﬁber shortening—ﬁber cutting due to\nshearing action, and (iv) ﬁnes formation—primary ﬁnes come from ray cells and parenchyma cells\nand microﬁbrils that are caused by ﬁber shortening or external ﬁbrillation. Moreover, the PFI reﬁning\ncould be adopted to obtain a higher internal ﬁbrillation than other laboratory reﬁners [1]. These eﬀects\nof the PFI reﬁning on cellulosic ﬁbers will improve the accessibility, the swelling, the ﬂexibility, and the\ninter-ﬁber bonding capacity of ﬁbers. It is assumed that these changes in the macro-level structure and\nproperties are related to the changes of crystallinity and H-bonding network during reﬁning [7,8].\n\nThere are some diﬀerent conclusions regarding to the eﬀects of PFI reﬁning on crystallinity of\ncellulose, not like that of ball milling, which eﬀectively reduces the crystallinity as the treatment\nprogresses. Therein,\nPapirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) reﬁning is the most common laboratory reﬁner in order to\nimprove the inter-ﬁber bonding capacity [1] and accessibility [2,3], and manufacture the micro-ﬁbrillated\nor nano-ﬁbrillated cellulose [4–6]. The main eﬀects of PFI reﬁning on ﬁbers are: (i) internal\nﬁbrillation—delaminating, loosening, and swelling of ﬁber wall; (ii) external ﬁbrillation—peeling of\nﬁbrils from the ﬁber surface while remaining attached; (iii) ﬁber shortening—ﬁber cutting due to\nshearing action, and (iv) ﬁnes formation—primary ﬁnes come from ray cells and parenchyma cells\nand microﬁbrils that are caused by ﬁber shortening or external ﬁbrillation. Cross-section model of cellulose crystallite for softwood ﬁbers and hardwood ﬁbers.\nIt is known that both the (110) and the (110) lattice plane are hydrophilic, and the (200)lattice\nplane is hydrophobic in cellulose Iβ (as Figure 5 shows). In addition, it is noticeable that the (110)\nplanes possess the highest theoretical roughness and accessibility to the hydrophilic groups in cellulose\nIβ [28]. Throughout the reﬁning of two pulp ﬁbers, the sizes perpendicular to (110) plane were more\nvolatile than the (110) plane and (200) plane, which is consistent with the report of Duchemin et al.,\nas shown in Table 1a,b [29]. It could be interpreted to be that water molecules were easier to permeate\nthrough the spaces between the hydrophilic (110) planes in paracrystalline region (hydration), and then\nit made these planes suﬀer more mechanical actions, so there was more adhesion (cocrystallization)\nand cleavage of cellulose chains created for (110) plane during PFI reﬁning.\nHowever, the crystallite size that was perpendicular to (200) lattice plane of two ﬁbers had an\nupward trend during PFI reﬁning. It could be explained in terms of coalescence of chains or some\ncrystallographic stacking of adjacent microﬁbrils, where the (200) planes were aligned upon drying [30].\n\nAdditionally, it was probably due to the weaker cleavage eﬀect on (200) lattice planes that was hard for\nwater molecules to penetrate.",
      "Polymers 2020, 12, 2912 2 of 14\nﬁrst and then decreased with the degree of reﬁning for hardwood bleached kraft pulp ﬁbers [11] or\nfor unbleached eucalyptus ﬁbers [12]. Moreover, Zhao et al. [7] reported that the crystallinity initially\nﬂuctuated upward and then downward, followed by a repeating ﬂuctuation with PFI reﬁning for\ntobacco stem mechanical pulp. None of the previous studies identiﬁed a clear trend, but the results\nwere that the crystallinity varied during PFI reﬁnement. Based on the large proportion of H-bonds in\ncrystalline region of cellulose, it can be assumed that the H-bonding network might change during\nPFI reﬁning.\nFourier transformation infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), which is sensitive to molecular structure,\ncan be as an indirect measurement for studying H-bonding network. FT-IR deconvolution of hydroxyl\ngroups band was adopted in order to study the changes of the energy of H-bonds and the H-bonding\ndistance during deligniﬁcation [13] or the deconstruction of cellulose [14]. Moreover, it was used\nto study the diﬀerences of the content of H-bonds not only between dislocation region and normal\nregion [15], but also among plant species [16,17]. Regarding the changes of H-bonding network during\nPFI reﬁning, Yuan et al. [18] reported that the content of H-bonds and crystallinity index (CI) of\neucalyptus ﬁbers changed with the increment of beating time. Subsequently, Zhao et al. [8] found that\nthe H-bonding energy for O(6)H· · · O(3′) inter-molecular H-bonds decreased by 12.9% and evolutions\nof the content of certain H-bonds diﬀered at various reﬁning stages.\n\nThere is still a lack of literature on the eﬀects of PFI reﬁnement on the H-bonding network.\nParticularly, the relationship between the content of H-bonds and crystallinity is still worthy of\nfurther study, which will deepen the understanding of the molecular aggregation and distribution of\nH-bonds, providing a molecular-scale explanation for the variations in accessibility, swelling, ﬂexibility,\nand ﬁbrillation of cellulosic ﬁbers during PFI reﬁnement. Therefore, this work explored the eﬀects\nof PFI reﬁnement on the CI, crystallite size, energy of H-bonds, H-bonding distance, and content of\nH-bonds for softwood pulp ﬁbers and hardwood pulp ﬁbers. Attempts were made in order to establish\nthe correlations between the CI and content of various H-bonds.",
      "2. Methods\n\n2.1. PFI Reﬁning\nCommercial bleached softwood and hardwood kraft pulp ﬁbers were obtained from\nZhongzhirenhe Company (Jinan, Shandong Province, China). Two pulp were treated with a PFI reﬁner\n(Hamjern Maskin A/S, Hamar, Norway) according to Tappi T248 wd-97, with a pulp consistency\nof 10%, the gap between the opposite reﬁning plates was 0.2 mm, and forces per bar length were\n3.33 N/mm and 1.77 N/mm for softwood ﬁbers and hardwood ﬁbers, respectively. The drainability was\ncharacterized by the Schopper Riegler number (SR-number) with the standards ISO 5267-1. Two pulp\nﬁbers were separately reﬁned in a PFI reﬁner at 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions and\nat 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions, respectively. Corresponding various pulps with an\nincreasing beating degree, such as 16, 20, 40, 63, and 79◦SR, were obtained for softwood ﬁbers and 0,\n26, 40, 57, and 70◦SR were obtained for hardwood ﬁbers.\n\n2.2. Morphological Analysis of Fibers and Mechanical Properties of Sheets\nThe ﬁnes content, weighted mean length, and macro-ﬁbrillation index of each sample were\ndetermined with a MORFI LB analyzer (Techpap SAS, Grenoble, France). The tensile strength of\ndry sheets and Wet-web strength were tested according to TAPPI T494 and Chinese standard GBT\n12914-2008, respectively. The zero-span tensile strength was tested with the Z-Span 2400 apparatus\n(Pulmac International Co. Ltd., Montpelier, VT, USA), according to the standard ISO 15361."
    ]
  }

MinerU85块＋全部既有优化 · 要点 2/3；边界 1/2

针叶木和阔叶木打浆后的纤维长度变化不一样。 [1]
PFI打浆过程中，针叶木和阔叶木的纤维长度均呈下降趋势。 [1]
针叶木的纤维长度在PFI打浆后变化显著。 [1]
阔叶木的纤维长度相对针叶木没有显著变化。 [1]
作者推测这种差别可能是因为阔叶木打浆时施加的 refining pressure 较低。 [1]

Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nThe trends of CI (CI-XI and CI-XA) for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers were all similar, decreasing first and then increasing, along with a decline, as shown in Figure 4. In the first refining stage, the decrease of the CI showed that mechanical treatment may mainly act in the crystalline region. Subsequently, the growth of the CI could be interpreted as greater force acting on the amorphous region in which cocrystallization might occur upon drying under the mechanical and thermal action of PFI refining. The subsequent decrease might be the continuous destruction of crystalline region.",

Effect of PFI Refining on Crystalline Index and Crystallite Size\n[原文]\nThe cellulose polymorph of these two fibers had no change during PFI treatment, which illustrates that the PFI refining is a relatively mild mechanical treatment, as the results of XRD in Online Resource (Figures S1 and S2) show. However, the CI-XI and the CI-XA were correlated significantly for both softwood fibers and hardwood fibers, with a correlation coefficient of 0.919 (p < 0.05) for softwood fibers and 0.925 (p < 0.05) for hardwood fibers, respectively, which is consistent with the report of Ahvenainen et al.       "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\nThere is still a lack of literature on the efects of PFI refinement on the H-bonding network. Particularly, the relationship between the content of H-bonds and crystallinity is still worthy of further study, which will deepen the understanding of the molecular aggregation and distribution of H-bonds, providing a molecular-scale explanation for the variations in accessibility, swelling, flexibility, and fibrillation of cellulosic fibers during PFI refinement. Therefore, this work explored the efects of PFI refinement on the CI, crystallite size, energy of H-bonds, H-bonding distance, and content of H-bonds for softwood pulp fibers and hardwood pulp fibers. PFI Refining\n[原文]\nCommercial bleached softwood and hardwood kraft pulp fibers were obtained from Zhongzhirenhe Company (Jinan, Shandong Province, China). Two pulp were treated with a PFI refiner (Hamjern Maskin A/S, Hamar, Norway) according to Tappi T248 wd-97, with a pulp consistency of 10%, the gap between the opposite refining plates was 0.2 mm, and forces per bar length were 3.33 N/mm and 1.77 N/mm for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers, respectively. The drainability was characterized by the Schopper Riegler number (SR-number) with the standards ISO 5267-1. Two pulp fibers were separately refined in a PFI refiner at 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions and at 0, 4000, 8000, 12,000, and 16,000 revolutions, respectively. Corresponding various pulps with an increasing beating degree, such as 16, 20, 40, 63, and 79<sup>◦</sup> SR, were obtained for softwood fibers and 0, 26, 40, 57, and 70<sup>◦</sup> SR were obtained for hardwood fibers.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 2. Methods > 2.2. Morphological Analysis of Fibers and Mechanical Properties of Sheets\n[原文]\nThe fines content, weighted mean length, and macro-fibrillation index of each sample were determined with a MORFI LB analyzer (Techpap SAS, Grenoble, France). Introduction\n[原文]\nMechanical, chemical, and biological treatments are usually adopted to obtain the desired physical and mechanical properties and for further utilization of the natural cellulosic fibers. Therein, Papirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) refining is the most common laboratory refiner in order to improve the inter-fiber bonding capacity [1] and accessibility [2,3], and manufacture the micro-fibrillated or nano-fibrillated cellulose [4–6]. The main efects of PFI refining on fibers are: (i) internal fibrillation—delaminating, loosening, and swelling of fiber wall; (ii) external fibrillation—peeling of fibrils from the fiber surface while remaining attached; (iii) fiber shortening—fiber cutting due to shearing action, and (iv) fines formation—primary fines come from ray cells and parenchyma cells and microfibrils that are caused by fiber shortening or external fibrillation. Moreover, the PFI refining could be adopted to obtain a higher internal fibrillation than other laboratory refiners [1]. These efects of the PFI refining on cellulosic fibers will improve the accessibility, the swelling, the flexibility, and the inter-fiber bonding capacity of fibers.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 1. Introduction\n[原文]\n It is assumed that these changes in the macro-level structure and properties are related to the changes of crystallinity and H-bonding network during refining [7,8].\n\nThere are some diferent conclusions regarding to the efects of PFI refining on crystallinity of cellulose, not like that of ball milling, which efectively reduces the crystallinity as the treatment progresses. Although some researchers considered that the crystallinity decreased during PFI refining for corn stover [9] or softwood pulp [10], some researchers reported that the crystallinity increased first and then decreased with the degree of refining for hardwood bleached kraft pulp fibers [11] or for unbleached eucalyptus fibers [12]. Moreover, Zhao et al. [7] reported that the crystallinity initially fluctuated upward and then downward, followed by a repeating fluctuation with PFI refining for tobacco stem mechanical pulp. None of the previous studies identified a clear trend, but the results were that the crystallinity varied during PFI refinement. Based on the large proportion of H-bonds in crystalline region of cellulose, it can be assumed that the H-bonding network might change during PFI refining.",
      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 4. Conclusions\n[原文]\nThe results indicated that the fibrillation and properties of fibers are related to the variation of the supramolecular structure during PFI refining. It is noticeable that there was a significantly positive correlation between the CI-XI and content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds during PFI refining for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers. Thus, the trend of the content of O(6)H· · · O(3)’ H-bonds might be generally speculated based on CI-XI while refining. Besides, the crystallite size, crystallinity, and content of various H-bonds did not change much in general. It is assumed that PFI refining is an excellent mechanical treatment of fibrillation with relatively little destruction on the supramolecular structure.\n\n[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 4. Thus, according to the crystallite sizes (as Table 1 shows) and the unit cell parameters of cellulose Iβ, there was most likely to be an average of two-fibrils with an arrangement of 234,432 packed side-by-side for both softwood fibers and hardwood fibers (as seen in Figure 5, drawn with mercury\n\n4.1.2 software). It decreased by 7.72% from 28.23% to 26.05% as refining from 0r to 4000 r and then increased by 9.14% from 4000 r to 8000 r, followed by a decrease of 17.13%, with the revolutions increasing from 8000 r to 16,000 r. Regarding the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds of hardwood fiber, the trend was almost similar to that of softwood fibers, except for a small increase of 0.45% from 8000 r to 12,000 r (in Table 2b). On the whole, the amount of the O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds for softwood fibers and hardwood fibers decreased by 16.54% and 5.91% altogether, respectively. The decrease might be due to the cleavage among cellulose molecular chains under the mechanical action of PFI refining, which was closely related to internal and external fibrillation (as seen in Section 3.1). On the other hand, the increase illustrates that there was not only the breakage, but also the formation of O(6)H···O(3′) H-bonds."

PyMuPDF结构81块基线 · 要点 3/3；边界 2/2

本文认为纸页抗张指数的提高主要来自PFI精磨过程中分丝帚化增强和细小组分增加，而不是单根纤维强度提高。 [1]
PFI精磨还会提高纤维润胀和分丝帚化，使纤维更柔顺并增强纤维间结合，从而提升纸页网络强度。 [2]
零距抗张指数通常用于表征纤维本身的抗张强度，因而可用于区分纸页强度与单根纤维强度。 [1]
零距抗张结果显示PFI精磨没有降低纤维强度，这与Kouko等的报道一致，但该结果并不表示纤维强度一定提高。 [1]
因此，纸页抗张性能提高可由分丝帚化、细小组分和纤维间结合改善解释；零距抗张在此用于检验纤维强度是否下降，并说明不能据此推断单纤维强度提高。 [1] [2]

  "answer": "本文认为纸页抗张指数的提高主要来自PFI精磨过程中分丝帚化增强和细小组分增加，而不是单根纤维强度提高。 [1]\nPFI精磨还会提高纤维润胀和分丝帚化，使纤维更柔顺并增强纤维间结合，从而提升纸页网络强度。 [2]\n零距抗张指数通常用于表征纤维本身的抗张强度，因而可用于区分纸页强度与单根纤维强度。 [1]\n零距抗张结果显示PFI精磨没有降低纤维强度，这与Kouko等的报道一致，但该结果并不表示纤维强度一定提高。 [1]\n因此，纸页抗张性能提高可由分丝帚化、细小组分和纤维间结合改善解释；零距抗张在此用于检验纤维强度是否下降，并说明不能据此推断单纤维强度提高。 [1] [2]",

      "Keywords: natural cellulosic ﬁbers; mechanical reﬁning; Crystallinity; Crystallite size;\nHydrogen bonds\n\n1. Introduction\nMechanical, chemical, and biological treatments are usually adopted to obtain the desired\nphysical and mechanical properties and for further utilization of the natural cellulosic ﬁbers. Therein,\nPapirindustriens forskningsinstitut (PFI) reﬁning is the most common laboratory reﬁner in order to\nimprove the inter-ﬁber bonding capacity [1] and accessibility [2,3], and manufacture the micro-ﬁbrillated\nor nano-ﬁbrillated cellulose [4–6]. The main eﬀects of PFI reﬁning on ﬁbers are: (i) internal\nﬁbrillation—delaminating, loosening, and swelling of ﬁber wall; (ii) external ﬁbrillation—peeling of\nﬁbrils from the ﬁber surface while remaining attached; (iii) ﬁber shortening—ﬁber cutting due to\nshearing action, and (iv) ﬁnes formation—primary ﬁnes come from ray cells and parenchyma cells\nand microﬁbrils that are caused by ﬁber shortening or external ﬁbrillation. Moreover, the PFI reﬁning\ncould be adopted to obtain a higher internal ﬁbrillation than other laboratory reﬁners [1]. These eﬀects\nof the PFI reﬁning on cellulosic ﬁbers will improve the accessibility, the swelling, the ﬂexibility, and the\ninter-ﬁber bonding capacity of ﬁbers. It is assumed that these changes in the macro-level structure and\nproperties are related to the changes of crystallinity and H-bonding network during reﬁning [7,8].\n\nThere are some diﬀerent conclusions regarding to the eﬀects of PFI reﬁning on crystallinity of\ncellulose, not like that of ball milling, which eﬀectively reduces the crystallinity as the treatment\nprogresses. Although some researchers considered that the crystallinity decreased during PFI reﬁning\nfor corn stover [9] or softwood pulp [10], some researchers reported that the crystallinity increased\nPolymers 2020, 12, 2912; doi:10.3390/polym12122912 www.mdpi.com/journal/polymers",
      "Polymers 2020, 12, 2912 10 of 14\nthe formation of O(6)H· · · O(3′) H-bonds. Both the fewer inter-molecular H-bonds and the lower CI\n(as Section 3.2 shows) will further improve the ﬂexibility of cellulosic ﬁbers, due to the higher mobility\nof molecular chains, the accessibility, and the WRV of ﬁbers (as seen in Section 3.1).\nAs to the O(3)H· · · O(5) intra-molecular H-bonds of softwood ﬁber, the content had a growth\nof 10.09% from 28.44% to 31.31% in the stage of reﬁning from 0 r to 4000 r, and then had a slight\ndecrease of 1.44% from 4000 r to 8000 r, followed by an increase of 13.16% until the end of reﬁning.\nOverall, the trend was similar to that of hardwood ﬁbers, which ﬁrst increased and then had a\ndecrease, followed by a growth. During the whole reﬁning, the amount of O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds for\nsoftwood ﬁbers and hardwood ﬁbers showed an upward tendency and increased by 22.78% and 8.8%,\nrespectively. The increase might be because the stable O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds might have not only\nless breakage under the action of water as destructor to the crystallites [30], but also creation in the\namorphous region upon drying. Because hydrogen bond–covalent bond synergies play an important\nrole in the cellulose stiﬀness axial modulus, more O(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds will enhance the cellulose\nstiﬀness [33,34].\n\nIn the case of the O(2)H· · · O(6) intra-molecular H-bonds for softwood ﬁber, the trend of content\ncan be described as two phases. It had an increase of 3.5% from 31.4% to 32.5% in the stage of reﬁning\nfrom 0 r to 4000 r and it then decreased by 21.57% from 4000 r to 12000 r, along with a growth of 15.26%\nin the last reﬁning stage. For the content of the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds of hardwood ﬁber, it increased\nﬁrstly and then had a decrease that was also followed by an increase. For both ﬁbers, the content of\nO(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds decreased, except for the stage of reﬁning from 0 r to 4000 r. It might be due to\nthe fact that the O(2)H· · · O(6) H-bonds, which are much more accessible to water, are less stable than\nO(3)H· · · O(5) H-bonds.\nAs to the free OH(2) and OH(6) of softwood fiber, the relative content showed a slight increase trend\nin general. The enhancement of the free OH(2) and OH(6) was understandable, because there was the\nbreakage of H-bonds among cellulosic molecules, which resulted in more extensive delamination and\nhigher specific surface area (as shown in Figure S4 and Table S1 in Online Resource). This made cellulose\nmore accessible to water and chemicals. However, for the free OH(2) and OH(6) of hardwood fiber,\nthe number of the free OH(2) and OH(6) decreased by 21.65% from 14.32% to 11.22%, with revolutions\nincreasing from 0 r to 4000 r, followed by an increase of 45.37% in the stage of refining from 4000 r to\n12,000 r, along with an decrease of 17.11%. It could be explained by the instability of free OH groups,\nwhich makes it easy to form new H-bonds, such as O(2)H···O(6) or O(6)H···O(3′)H-bonds. MinerU85块＋全部既有优化 · 要点 3/3；边界 2/2

本文把纸页抗张强度的提高主要归因于 PFI 精磨过程中细纤维化（fibrillation）和细组分（fines）的增加。 [1]
文中指出 PFI 精磨改善了细纤维化（尤其内部细纤维化）和纤维润胀，并提高了纸页抗张强度，同时纤维抗张强度没有下降。 [1]
零距抗张指数通常用于表征纤维的拉伸强度，文中据此检验精磨后单根纤维的强度。 [1]
零距抗张结果显示 PFI 精磨未降低纤维强度；因此该结果支持“纤维强度未下降”，但不能据此认定单根纤维强度一定提高。 [1]

  "answer": "本文把纸页抗张强度的提高主要归因于 PFI 精磨过程中细纤维化（fibrillation）和细组分（fines）的增加。 [1]\n文中指出 PFI 精磨改善了细纤维化（尤其内部细纤维化）和纤维润胀，并提高了纸页抗张强度，同时纤维抗张强度没有下降。 [1]\n零距抗张指数通常用于表征纤维的拉伸强度，文中据此检验精磨后单根纤维的强度。 [1]\n零距抗张结果显示 PFI 精磨未降低纤维强度；因此该结果支持“纤维强度未下降”，但不能据此认定单根纤维强度一定提高。 [1]",

      "[章节标签（程序整理，非原文）] 2. Methods > 2.1. PFI Refining\n[原文]\nCommercial bleached softwood and hardwood kraft pulp fibers were obtained from Zhongzhirenhe Company (Jinan, Shandong Province, China).
